info.desc: The Stooges is the self-titled debut studio album by American rock band The Stooges. It was released in August 1969 on Elektra Records. Two songs, "I Wanna Be Your Dog" and "1969", were released as singles and the album peaked at number 106 on the Billboard album charts. It is widely considered one of the best Garage Rock albums. With Ron Asheton's walls of distortion, and distorted wah wah solos, textures and power chord riffs it is also considered to have had an impact on Hard Rock. podcast.body: Produced by John Cale of The Velvet Underground, this debut album was a minimalist manifesto. It featured dirty guitars, monotonous rhythms, and lyrics that explored carnal desire, apathy, and an existential void, marking a deliberate rejection of sophisticated and virtuous sounds in favor of raw noise. "Su debut, Destuji, producido por John K. L. De Debel, Betander Brown, fue un manifiesto minimalista de guitarras sucias, Rhythm Monotónos y letras que hablaban de desear carnal, abatía y vacío existencial."

podcast.body: This 1969 debut album from Iggy Pop and the Stooges is characterized as "very aggressive post garage rock." The band was known for being "drugged out, whacked out, and totally crazy" and was considered the most important of the post-Garage Rock bands, continuing to resonate when the original sound had largely faded. "Iggy Pop and the Stooges from their 1969 debut album, very aggressive post garage rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.body: This album was produced by John Cale of The Velvet Underground. Due to the band's inability to rehearse for more than 20 minutes, half the material was allegedly written the night before their first day in the studio, with old avant-garde ideas reworked into more coherent songs. The initial mix was rejected by Elektra president Jack Holtzman, who then re-mixed it himself, but despite this, the album did not sell well as it was considered too raw and primitive for most people at the time. "Nobody was making music that sounded like this."
